mcqs.question: According to Tony Hoare's own framing, what exactly was the "billion-dollar mistake" — the concept of null itself, or something else?
options: The mistake was implementing multiple different null values for different types instead of one universal null
The mistake was making null representable for every reference type simply because it was easy to implement, with no separate type-level tracking of which values could actually be absent
The mistake was that null cannot be represented in any type system at all
The mistake was choosing the specific keyword "null" instead of a different name
mcqs.explanation: Hoare's own account is that representing absence was a legitimate need, but making it silently available on every reference type with no type-level distinction was the actual error — the type promised more than it guaranteed. Null is very much representable in type systems (that's the whole subject of this Topic), the mistake wasn't about multiple null values, and it has nothing to do with naming.

mcqs.question: `findUser(id)` is declared to return `String` but sometimes returns null. The caller compiles cleanly and later crashes with a NullPointerException. Why didn't the type checker catch this?
options: Because the type checker only runs on code paths that have been unit tested

Because String, without a nullability marker, doesn't distinguish "definitely a string" from "a string, or possibly nothing," so the checker sees a type match and has no signal that this value might be absent
Because NullPointerException is always a compiler bug, not a real runtime condition
Because the function was declared with the wrong number of parameters
mcqs.explanation: A plain String type in a null-permissive language carries no information about nullability, so the checker genuinely cannot see a problem — the type signature itself is the gap being exploited. The type checker runs statically regardless of test coverage, NullPointerException is a legitimate runtime condition, and this scenario has nothing to do with parameter count.

mcqs.question: In Kotlin, why does `greet(null)` fail to compile when `greet` is declared as `fun greet(name: String)`?
options: Because Kotlin disallows calling any function with a null literal anywhere in the language
Because greet has no parameters accepting null under any type
Because String requires a non-empty string literal at every call site
Because plain String in Kotlin is non-nullable by default, and null is only a valid value for a type explicitly marked nullable with String?
mcqs.explanation: Kotlin's null-safe-by-default design excludes null from plain String automatically; only the explicitly marked String? type accepts null, and greet's parameter isn't marked that way. Kotlin does allow null literals where a nullable type is expected, greet does have one parameter (just non-nullable), and there's no such empty-string-literal restriction.

mcqs.question: A developer wraps a return type in `Optional<User>` but then calls `.get()` on it at every call site without checking `.isPresent()` first. Does this actually eliminate the null-pointer-style bug the wrapping was meant to prevent?
options: Yes — Optional automatically prevents any crash regardless of how it's used
No — calling .get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException at that exact line, which is functionally the same crash as the NullPointerException it was meant to replace
Yes, because Optional.get() always returns a default value instead of throwing
No, because Optional<T> cannot be empty once constructed
mcqs.explanation: Optional gives the type system the vocabulary to express absence, but it can't force safe usage — an unchecked .get() on an empty Optional throws just as reliably as a null dereference would have, defeating the purpose. It does not guarantee crash prevention regardless of usage, .get() throws rather than defaulting, and an Optional can absolutely be empty by design.

mcqs.question: Why hasn't Java simply changed its default so that plain reference types are non-nullable, the way Kotlin does?
options: Java's entire existing ecosystem assumes any reference might be null, and changing that default would break assumptions baked into decades of existing code and libraries
Java's compiler is technically incapable of tracking nullability in any way
Non-nullable types are impossible to express in a language with type erasure
Because null-permissive typing is strictly safer than null-safe-by-default typing
mcqs.explanation: The real barrier is migration cost across a massive existing ecosystem built on null-permissive assumptions, not a technical limitation — which is why Java added optional, non-default tools (Optional<T>, external @Nullable annotations) instead of changing the meaning of a plain reference type. Java's tooling can and does track nullability via these add-ons, type erasure is unrelated to expressing non-nullability, and null-permissive typing is not safer — it's the exact problem this Topic addresses.
